lnx1.html: The shell (bash) is a program that reads commands you type and runs them. Every command is name [options] [arguments]. Options start with - (-l) or -- (--all). The prompt ends in $ for a normal user.

Everything hangs off the root /. Your files live in your home directory, /home/phil, which the shell abbreviates as ~.

  • Absolute path starts at /: /home/phil/notes.md.
  • Relative path starts from where you are: notes.md, projects/app.py.
  • . = here, .. = one level up, ~ = home.

CommandDoes
pwdPrint working directory (where am I?)
lsList files. ls -l long/details, ls -a include hidden (dotfiles), ls -la both
cd DIRChange directory. cd alone → home, cd .. → up, cd - → previous
cat FILEPrint a file's contents
less FILEPage through a long file (q to quit)
head -n 5 / tail -n 5First / last 5 lines
treeShow the directory as a tree
man CMDThe manual for any command
Pro habitWhen lost: pwd to see where you are, ls to see what's here, cd to move. That loop never fails.
Files starting with . (like .bashrc) are hidden; ls -a shows them. In a real terminal, press Tab to auto-complete a name — type cd Doc then Tab. The lab terminal supports Tab too.

lnx1.h: Deep dive: moving around like you live here
lnx1.html:
/home/phil/projects/app.py     # absolute: starts at /
projects/app.py                # relative: from where you are now
../Documents                   # .. = parent, . = here, ~ = your home

mkdir -p work/2026/reports     # -p creates missing parents, no error if it exists
cp -r projects projects-copy   # -r copies a directory tree
mv draft.txt final.txt         # mv renames…
mv final.txt ~/Documents/      # …and moves
rm -r old-folder               # recursive delete — there is no recycle bin
ls -la                         # long listing including hidden .dotfiles
tree                           # the whole tree at a glance
  • Globs are expanded by the shell before the command runs: *.pdf, report-?.txt, [ab]*. Run echo *.pdf to preview what a glob matches before handing it to rm.
  • Linux is case-sensitive: Notes.txt and notes.txt are different files.
  • Key places: /etc (config), /var/log (logs), /home (users), /tmp (scratch), /usr/bin (programs), /root (the admin's home).
  • file x says what a file is; stat x shows size, permissions and times.

lnx2.html:
Every command has stdin (input), stdout (output) and stderr (errors). Three operators rewire them:

  • | pipe: send one command's stdout into the next command's stdin. cat log | grep ERROR.
  • > redirect stdout to a file (overwrite); >> append. ls > files.txt.
  • < read stdin from a file.
The Unix philosophyEach tool does one thing well. Power comes from piping them together. A pro builds a pipeline left to right, checking the output at each |.

grep ERROR app.log           # lines containing ERROR
grep -i error app.log        # case-insensitive
grep -v INFO app.log         # lines WITHOUT INFO
grep -c ERROR app.log        # count matching lines
grep -n ERROR app.log        # show line numbers
grep -r TODO projects/       # recurse into a directory

• cut -d, -f3 sales.csv — field 3 of a comma-delimited file.
  • sort (alphabetical), sort -n (numeric), sort -r (reverse).
  • uniq -c — collapse adjacent duplicates and count. Always sort | uniq.
  • wc -l count lines, -w words, -c chars.

The classic "top values" one-liner:

cut -d, -f2 sales.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

• sed edits a stream. sed 's/old/new/g' replaces all old with new on each line. sed -n '2,5p' prints lines 2–5. sed '/DEBUG/d' deletes matching lines.
  • awk works with columns. Fields are $1 $2 …, whole line is $0, line number is NR. awk -F, '$2=="West" {print $3}' prints column 3 where column 2 is West. awk -F, 'NR>1 {s+=$4} END {print s}' sums column 4.
Quote trapWrap awk/sed programs in single quotes so the shell doesn't expand $4 before awk sees it.

lnx2.h: Deep dive: the three streams and composing tools
lnx2.html:
Every program has stdin (0), stdout (1) and stderr (2). Pipes connect stdout to the next stdin; errors go to the screen unless you redirect them.

cmd > out.txt          # stdout to a file (overwrite)
cmd >> out.txt         # append
cmd 2> errors.txt      # stderr only
cmd > all.txt 2>&1     # both streams into one file
cmd 2>/dev/null        # discard errors
cmd | tee copy.txt | wc -l   # save a copy AND keep piping
ls *.log | xargs wc -l       # turn lines of input into arguments

# CSV columns: skip the header, pick a column, count unique values
tail -n +2 sales.csv | cut -d, -f2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
  • sort -t, -k4 -n sorts a CSV by its 4th column numerically.
  • uniq only collapses adjacent duplicates — always sort first.
  • tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' translates characters; tr -d '\r' strips Windows line endings.
  • Exit codes: 0 = success. a && b runs b only if a succeeded; a || b only if it failed.

lnx3.html:
name="Phil"          # no spaces around =
echo "Hi $name"      # $ expands it → Hi Phil
export PATH="$PATH:~/bin"   # export makes it available to child programs

$HOME, $USER, $PATH (where the shell looks for commands), $PWD, $? (exit status of the last command: 0 = success). See all with env.

ls -l shows -rwxr-xr--: type, then owner/group/others each with read(4) write(2) execute(1).

chmod 755 file    # rwx r-x r-x  (owner all, others read+exec)
chmod 644 file    # rw- r-- r--  (typical file)
chmod u+x file    # add execute for the owner
chmod go-w file   # remove write from group & others

Octal: add the numbers — rwx = 4+2+1 = 7, r-x = 5, r-- = 4. A script needs execute (chmod +x) to run as ./script.sh.

#!/bin/bash           # "shebang": run this file with bash
echo "Backing up..."
for f in *.txt; do    # loop over matching files
  echo "Found $f"
done

if [ -f config.ini ]; then   # test: does the file exist?
  echo "config present"
fi

$1 $2 … are command-line arguments, $# is how many, $@ is all of them. Make it executable (chmod +x run.sh) and run ./run.sh.

• find . -name "*.log" -type f — search recursively by name/type.
  • find . -name "*.tmp" -delete — find and act.
  • Globs: * any chars, ? one char, [abc] a set. ls *.py, ls app?.js.
  • alias ll="ls -la" — shortcuts (put in ~/.bashrc).
  • && run next only if the last succeeded; ; run regardless.

lnx3.h: Try it for real: your first script
lnx3.html:
The lab terminal has a built-in editor. Type nano hello.sh, write the script, tap Save, then run it.

#!/bin/bash
# hello.sh — greet the current user
name="$USER"
echo "Hello, $name"
echo "You are in $(pwd)"
bash hello.sh        # run it with bash (no permission needed)
chmod +x hello.sh    # or make it executable…
./hello.sh           # …and run it directly (./ = "in this folder")
  • $(command) inserts a command's output: today=$(date).
  • $((2 + 3)) does integer math.
  • Quote your variables: "$file" keeps names with spaces in one piece.
  • Single quotes are literal: echo '$HOME' prints $HOME; double quotes expand: echo "$HOME" prints /home/phil.

lnx4.html:
awk reads input one line (record) at a time, splits it into fields, and runs every rule whose pattern matches.

awk 'PATTERN { ACTION }' file

awk '$4 == 404' access.log            # pattern only → print matching lines
awk '{ print $1 }' access.log          # action only → runs on every line
awk '$4 >= 400 { print $1, $3 }' access.log
  • $0 is the whole line; $1…$NF are fields; NF = number of fields, so $NF is the last one.
  • NR = current line number (record number) across all input.
  • Fields split on runs of whitespace by default. -F, (or BEGIN{FS=","}) splits on commas.
  • In print a, b the comma inserts OFS (a space by default). print a b with no comma concatenates.
Always single-quotethe program. Inside double quotes the shell would expand $1 before awk ever saw it.

Variables need no declaration; they start as 0 / empty string. BEGIN runs before any input, END after the last line — the place to print totals.

awk '{ bytes += $5 } END { print bytes }' access.log

awk 'BEGIN { print "ip,status" } { print $1 "," $4 }' access.log

awk -F, 'NR > 1 { units += $4 } END { print "units:", units }' sales.csv

NR > 1 is the standard trick to skip a CSV header. Forget it and the header row sneaks into your report.

Averages: END { print total / NR } — or divide by your own counter when a pattern filtered lines.

awk arrays are keyed by strings. That makes "count per X" and "sum per X" one-liners — the shell equivalent of SQL GROUP BY.

# requests per status code
awk '{ c[$4]++ } END { for (s in c) print s, c[s] }' access.log

# bytes per client IP
awk '{ b[$1] += $5 } END { for (ip in b) print ip, b[ip] }' access.log

# revenue per region (units × price), skipping the header
awk -F, 'NR>1 { r[$2] += $4 * $5 } END { for (k in r) print k, r[k] }' sales.csv

for (k in arr) visits keys in no guaranteed order — pipe into sort when order matters. if (k in arr) tests membership without creating the key.

awk '$2 == "POST" && $4 == 401 { fails[$1]++ }
     END { for (ip in fails) if (fails[ip] >= 2) print ip, fails[ip] }' access.log

awk '{ if ($4 >= 500) err++; else if ($4 >= 400) warn++ }
     END { print "5xx:", err+0, "4xx:", warn+0 }' access.log

awk -F, 'NR>1 { printf "%-8s %8.2f\n", $2, $4*$5 }' sales.csv
  • Operators: == != < <= > >=, && || !, regex match $3 ~ /login/ and !~.
  • printf does not add a newline — write \n yourself. %s string, %d integer, %.2f two decimals, %-8s left-pad to width 8.
  • err+0 forces a number, so an unset counter prints 0 instead of an empty string.
  • Built-ins: length($0), substr(s, start, len), index(s, t), split(s, arr, sep), toupper(), tolower(), int(), sprintf().
  • next skips to the next line; exit stops reading (END still runs).

lnx4.h: Reading the logs like a defender
lnx4.html:
These one-liners are how you answer incident questions fast, on any Linux box, with no extra tools installed:

QuestionPipeline
Who is hitting us most?awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
Which IPs keep failing login?awk '$3=="/login" && $4==401 {f[$1]++} END{for(i in f) print f[i], i}' access.log | sort -rn
How much traffic did we serve?awk '{s+=$5} END{print s}' access.log
Any server errors?awk '$4 >= 500' access.log
Defender mindsetA burst of 401s from one IP is the signature of password guessing. Spotting it in your own logs is exactly the skill a SOC analyst uses; acting on it (block, alert, report) is the job.

lnx5.html:
sed reads lines, applies commands, and prints the result. Each command can have an address that limits which lines it touches.

sed 's/old/new/'   file     # first match on each line
sed 's/old/new/g'  file     # every match on each line
sed 's/error/ERR/gi' file    # g = global, i = ignore case
sed '3d'           file     # delete line 3
sed '/^#/d'        file     # delete comment lines
sed -n '5,10p'     file     # print only lines 5–10
sed -n '/ERROR/p'  file     # grep-like
sed '2,/end/d'     file     # range: line 2 through the first line matching end
sed '/keep/!d'     file     # ! negates: delete everything EXCEPT keep
sed '10q'          file     # print the first 10 lines then quit (like head)

Join several commands with ; or repeat -e: sed -e '/^#/d' -e 's/a/b/'.

sed 's/web/&-server/'                  # & = whatever matched → web-server01
sed 's/^\([a-z]*\)\([0-9]*\)/\2-\1/'    # BRE groups \( \) → 01-web
sed -E 's/^([a-z]+)([0-9]+)/\2-\1/'      # -E: extended regex, plain ( ) +
sed -E 's/(up|down)/[\1]/'

-i rewrites the file in place — no output, the file just changes.

cp app.conf app.conf.bak                 # ALWAYS back up first
sed -i 's/^port=8080$/port=9090/' app.conf
sed -i '/^#/d' app.conf
diff app.conf.bak app.conf               # review exactly what changed
Pro habitRun the sed without -i first and read the output. Anchor patterns (^port=) so you change only the line you mean — s/8080/9090/ would also hit proxy_port=18080.

find /var/log -type f -name "*.log"       # files by name (quote the glob!)
find . -iname "readme*"                  # case-insensitive
find . -maxdepth 1 -type d               # only the top level
find /tmp -type f -empty                 # zero-byte files
find . -size +100M                       # bigger than 100 MB (k, M, G)
find . -type f ! -name "*.txt"           # ! negates a test
find . -perm 777                         # world-writable — a security red flag
find . -name "*.log" -exec grep -c ERROR {} \;   # run a command per file
find /tmp -type f -empty -delete         # act on the results

Tests are ANDed left to right. {} is replaced by each path; \; ends the -exec command (the backslash stops the shell eating the ;).

-delete safelyRun the exact find without -delete first, read the list, then add -delete at the end. Put it earlier and it deletes before your filters apply.

grep -r ERROR srv/            # search a whole tree (prefixes file names)
grep -rh ERROR srv/           # -h: hide file names (for piping)
grep -rl ERROR srv/           # -l: only list which files match
grep -c ERROR a.log b.log     # count per file
grep -w timeout log           # whole word only
grep -E "401|403" access.log  # extended regex alternation
grep -v INFO app.log          # invert: everything except INFO

Every command returns an exit status: 0 = success, non-zero = failure (grep returns 1 when nothing matched). Chain on it:

grep -q ERROR app.log && echo "errors found"
cd /srv/app || echo "missing dir"
command 2>/dev/null           # throw away error messages
command > out.txt 2>&1        # stdout AND stderr into one file

Real questions, answered in one line each:

# Which log files exist under /srv?
find /srv -type f -name "*.log"

# How many ERROR lines across all of them?
grep -rh ERROR /srv | wc -l

# What is the most common error message?
grep -rh ERROR /srv | cut -d" " -f3- | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -1

# Skip a header, then the top 3 values of column 4
tail -n +2 sales.csv | sort -t, -k4 -nr | head -3

Read them left to right: find the data → filter (grep/awk) → shape (cut/sed) → aggregate (sort/uniq -c/awk arrays) → rank & trim (sort -rn, head). That pattern covers most log questions you will ever be asked.

lnx6.html:
#!/bin/bash
# count.sh PATTERN FILE
if [ $# -lt 2 ]; then            # $# = number of arguments
  echo "usage: $0 PATTERN FILE"   # $0 = script name
  exit 1                         # non-zero = failure
fi
pattern=$1; file=$2
if [ ! -f "$file" ]; then
  echo "no such file: $file"; exit 2
fi
echo "$(grep -c "$pattern" "$file") matches"
TestTrue when
-f F / -d D / -e Pfile / directory / anything exists
-z "$s" / -n "$s"string empty / not empty
"$a" = "$b" / !=strings equal / differ
$x -eq 5 -ne -lt -le -gt -genumeric comparisons

$@ is all arguments (quote it: "$@"). Every command returns an exit code — if just checks it, so if grep -q ERROR log; then works with no brackets.

for f in logs/*.log; do         # over files
  echo "$(wc -l < "$f") $f"
done

for i in {1..5}; do echo $i; done   # over a range

while read -r name status load; do  # over lines, split into fields
  if [ "$status" = "down" ]; then echo "DOWN $name"; fi
done < servers.txt

count=0
count=$((count + 1))            # arithmetic
(( count > 3 )) && echo "many"

break leaves a loop, continue skips to the next item. Redirect a whole loop: done > report.txt.

log() { echo "[$(date +%H:%M)] $*"; }    # define
backup() {
  local src=$1                           # local to the function
  cp "$src" "$src.bak" || return 1        # return an exit code
}
backup app.conf && log "backed up"
  • set -euo pipefail at the top of real scripts: stop on errors (-e), on unset variables (-u), and on failures inside pipes (pipefail).
  • Quote every variable ("$file") — unquoted variables split on spaces and expand globs.
  • Default values: ${1:-servers.txt}. String length: ${#name}.
  • trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT cleans up temp files even on failure; getopts parses -v -o file style options.
  • Run ShellCheck on scripts — it catches most quoting and logic bugs automatically.
  • Never put passwords in scripts; read secrets from protected files or environment, and keep scripts writable only by their owner.

lnx7.html:
ps aux | grep nginx          # every process; find one
top   /   htop               # live CPU / memory view
kill 1234                    # polite stop (SIGTERM, 15)
kill -9 1234                 # force kill (SIGKILL) — last resort, no cleanup

systemctl status sshd        # is the service running? recent log lines
sudo systemctl restart nginx
sudo systemctl enable --now nginx   # start now AND at boot
journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago"   # that service's logs
journalctl -p err -b         # errors since this boot

id                       # your uid, gid and groups
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash ana    # create a user with a home
sudo passwd ana
sudo usermod -aG developers ana      # -a append! without it you REPLACE groups
sudo chown ana:developers report.txt
sudo -l                  # what am I allowed to run with sudo?
  • /etc/passwd: accounts (readable by all). /etc/shadow: password hashes (root only). /etc/group: groups. /etc/sudoers (edit only with visudo).
  • Least privilege: give people the groups and sudo rules they need, nothing more; disable direct root login over SSH.

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade     # Debian/Ubuntu
sudo dnf install httpd                   # RHEL/Fedora
df -h                 # free space per filesystem
du -sh /var/log/*     # what is using it
ip a                  # interfaces and IP addresses
ip route              # default gateway
ss -tulpn             # listening ports and which process owns them
ping -c 3 8.8.8.8     # basic reachability
curl -I https://example.com   # HTTP headers
dig example.com       # DNS lookup

ssh-keygen -t ed25519            # create a key pair (~/.ssh/id_ed25519 + .pub)
ssh-copy-id ana@server           # install the PUBLIC key in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
ssh ana@server                   # log in with the key
scp report.txt ana@server:/tmp/  # copy a file over SSH

crontab -e       # edit your scheduled jobs
# ┌ minute (0-59)  ┌ hour (0-23)  ┌ day of month  ┌ month  ┌ day of week (0-7, Sun=0 or 7)
  30            2              *               *        *      /home/ana/backup.sh
  */15          *              *               *        *      /home/ana/check.sh
  0             9              *               *        1-5    /home/ana/report.sh

Private keys never leave your machine (chmod 600); only the .pub file is shared. Harden SSH with key-only login (PasswordAuthentication no) and PermitRootLogin no.
